channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The IMF now expects global GDP to grow 3% in 2026, down from 3.3% in January, yet the feared collapse from the Strait of Hormuz crisis has not materialised — the eurozone grew 0.4% in the second quarter and no sharp downturn is forecast.
item.description:
The revision is modest and the tone reassuring. The International Monetary Fund cut its 2026 global growth forecast to 3% from 3.3% in January, but stressed the world economy has proved more resilient than expected: the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20% of global hydrocarbons flow, did not trigger the collapse many feared, and Europe posted 0.4% growth in the second quarter. Neither the economist consensus nor major institutions expect a pronounced decline in activity, even amid the Iran war, tariff turmoil and sanctions. The message is one of slower but steady global expansion rather than recession — a backdrop that still carries obvious downside risks from energy shocks and trade conflict.

Industry Impact

For chemical and Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) producers, a 3% global-growth backdrop means demand keeps expanding but at a cooler pace, so volume planning should assume steady rather than accelerating end-markets. The resilience to the Hormuz shock is encouraging for feedstock stability, but the same report's caveats — energy, tariffs, geopolitics — are precisely the ACS cost and demand risks running through this alert. The practical read is to plan for moderate growth while keeping contingency for the energy-price and trade-policy shocks that could still knock the outlook off course.

Les Echos

item.title: Large container ships are returning to the Suez Canal after almost 1,000 days of Houthi-driven diversions around the Cape of Good Hope, as lines restore Asia–Europe services ahead of the peak shipping season, cutting transit times and costs.
item.description:
The key east–west artery is reopening to big ships. Major container lines are beginning to restore services through the Suez Canal as peak-season shipments to Europe and the US build, after nearly 1,000 days during which attacks on commercial vessels by Yemen's Houthi forces from late 2023 pushed carriers onto the longer, costlier route around the Cape of Good Hope. The return of mega vessels shortens sailing times and lowers freight costs on the Asia–Europe lane, and is described as a clear positive for exporters shipping time-sensitive goods such as apparel, textiles and engineering products. It marks a tentative normalisation of a trade route whose disruption has weighed on global supply-chain costs for over two years.

Industry Impact

Ocean freight cost and reliability feed directly into landed input costs and delivery times for chemical and Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) producers moving raw materials and finished goods between Asia and Europe. A return to Suez trims the extra days and expense that Cape routing added, easing working-capital and inventory pressure and improving service to European customers. The normalisation is still tentative and security-dependent, so it is a welcome offset — especially against Europe's low-water Rhine disruptions — rather than a settled all-clear; supply-chain planners should treat the improvement as real but reversible.

The Hindu Business Line

item.title: Vietnam's economy grew 8.4% year-on-year in the second quarter and 8.2% in the first half, with exports up 21% to USD 266.5bn and FDI up 61%, while the ASEAN-5 posted a combined USD 156.6bn trade surplus in 2025.
item.description:
Southeast Asia's momentum held. Vietnam expanded 8.4% year-on-year in the second quarter and 8.2% over the first half, driven by recovering domestic demand and strength in manufacturing, construction and industry; first-half exports rose 21% to USD 266.5bn and foreign investment jumped 61% to USD 34.7bn. Zooming out, UOB research found the five main ASEAN economies — Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam — recorded a combined trade surplus of USD 156.6bn in 2025, extending an eleven-year growth trend, with resilient intra-ASEAN trade of about USD 63bn underpinned by integrated regional supply chains. The bloc is cementing its position as a manufacturing and trade hub as companies diversify away from concentration risk elsewhere.

Industry Impact

Southeast Asia is a structural growth region for the construction, automotive, electronics and consumer-manufacturing demand that pulls through adhesives, coatings and sealants, so Vietnam's high-single-digit growth and the ASEAN-5's expanding trade base strengthen the medium-term demand and investment case for ACS producers there. Rising manufacturing and FDI, plus integrated regional supply chains, point to specific opportunities in electronics assembly, packaging and construction. For suppliers weighing where to add capacity as North American and China routes get harder, ASEAN increasingly looks like the region to prioritise.

VietnamPlus | VietnamPlus

item.title: Germany's federal police put 2025 cybercrime damage at EUR 202.4bn, about 4.5% of GDP, with ransomware up 10%, while OpenAI warned of "ongoing, persistent" AI-enabled cyber-attacks, many stemming from open-source models developed in China.
item.description:
The scale is striking. The Federal Criminal Police Office's Cybercrime 2025 report estimated damage to the German economy at EUR 202.4 billion — roughly 4.5% of GDP — with around 335,000 recorded cases, ransomware incidents up 10% to 1,041, and attacks on service availability up 25% to over 36,700; a large share originated abroad or from unknown locations. Separately, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane warned that organisations should prepare for "ongoing, persistent" cyber-attacks powered by AI, flagging risk from open-source models — many developed in China — that trail frontier systems by only months. OpenAI has paused training of some frontier models while it adds safeguards. Together the reports underline how quickly the industrial cyber-threat is escalating.

Industry Impact

Manufacturers, including chemical and Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) producers, are squarely in the target set: connected plants, operational-technology systems and supply-chain software are exactly what ransomware and availability attacks disrupt, and a hit can halt production, corrupt formulations data or expose intellectual property. AI-accelerated attacks lower the cost and raise the frequency of intrusions, so the practical takeaway is to harden operational-technology security, patch and segment plant networks, rehearse incident response and vet software suppliers. Cyber-resilience is now an operational-continuity issue for industrial firms, not just an IT budget line.

Initiative Mittelstand | The Guardian

item.title: Rheinmetall (over EUR 100bn) and naval builder TKMS (over EUR 25bn) together hold more than EUR 125bn in defence orders, and attention is shifting to securing the raw materials and inputs needed to deliver Europe's rearmament.
item.description:
Germany's two defence champions are sitting on record backlogs. Rheinmetall expects an order book above EUR 100bn by 2026, and TKMS, the naval specialist spun out to focus on submarines and surface ships, now exceeds EUR 25bn including a frigate programme booked after the balance-sheet date — together more than EUR 125bn. With demand locked in by European rearmament and the war in Ukraine, the binding constraint is moving from orders to execution: securing metals, specialty chemicals, electronics and other inputs, and the industrial capacity to convert the backlog into deliveries. That makes the supply chain, not the order pipeline, the story to watch for the defence-industrial build-out.

Industry Impact

Defence and aerospace are high-specification markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants — structural bonding, protective and signature coatings, sealing and corrosion protection on vehicles, ships and munitions — so a EUR 125bn backlog points to durable, multi-year demand for qualified ACS products in Europe. The explicit focus on raw materials signals both opportunity and competition for inputs, as defence primes compete for the same metals, resins and specialty chemicals that civil industry uses. ACS suppliers with defence-qualified products and secure feedstock positions stand to benefit, while others may feel tighter availability and firmer pricing on shared inputs.

Wallstreet:online

item.title: China's industrial value-added rose 5.3% in January–July, with high-tech "new growth drivers" supplying nearly half of first-half industrial growth, as Shanghai's property easing took effect and a new national urban-renewal plan was issued.
item.description:
The domestic picture stayed resilient. National Bureau of Statistics estimates put industrial value-added of enterprises above designated size up 5.3% year-on-year over the first seven months, and separately showed that high-tech manufacturing and digital-product "new kinetic energy" contributed nearly 50% of industrial growth in the first half from just over 20% of value added — evidence of a shift toward higher-tech output. On property, Shanghai's "Eight Articles" took effect on 21 August, optimising provident-fund withdrawals and mortgages, adding trade-in purchase subsidies and housing vouchers, and supporting second-hand-home acquisition; agents reported busier viewings. Beijing also issued its 15th Five-Year Plan for urban renewal, emphasising heritage protection and organic renewal over demolition.

Industry Impact

Construction, real estate and manufacturing are among the largest end-markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants, so firm Chinese industrial output plus fresh property-demand measures support volumes for construction chemicals and industrial ACS. The tilt toward urban renewal and renovation — rather than only new build — steers demand toward repair, retrofit and refurbishment products, while the high-tech growth-driver shift points to rising materials demand in electronics and advanced manufacturing. Together these signal where China's ACS-linked demand will concentrate: upgrade and renovation projects, and higher-specification industrial applications rather than a broad construction boom.

Xhby.net | China Economic Net | China Economic Net | China Economic Net

item.title: South Korea's trade commission issued a preliminary ruling to impose anti-dumping duties on imported solid caustic soda from China and Taiwan, with Formosa Plastics facing 38.89% and Chinese producers 3.66–22.21%, a direct chemical trade-defence action.
item.description:
The Korea Trade Commission's preliminary finding targets solid sodium hydroxide (caustic soda), a basic industrial chemical, imported from Taiwan and mainland China. Anti-dumping duties — extra import taxes meant to counter below-cost pricing — were proposed at 38.89% for Taiwan's Formosa Plastics, and at 3.66% for China's Binzhou Chemical, 19.93% for Tianjin Unilion Supply Chain, 22.21% for Sky Impex and 17.58% for others. Formosa Plastics said it has already adjusted its solid caustic soda sales strategy and is exploring other markets including Japan, the US, Europe, Australia and Southeast Asia. The case adds to a run of Asian chemical trade-defence moves and shows how quickly duty exposure can shift by exporter and country.

Industry Impact

This is a concrete chemical-sector signal for Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) and chemicals buyers: caustic soda is a widely used feedstock and processing chemical, and anti-dumping duties of up to nearly 39% will reshape who supplies it into South Korea and where displaced Chinese and Taiwanese volumes go next — potentially pressuring prices in Japan, Europe, Southeast Asia and beyond as producers redirect exports. It underlines a broader pattern of proliferating trade-defence duties on specialty and commodity chemicals across Asia, so ACS producers should track duty scope by exporting entity and country and factor redirected trade flows into raw-material sourcing and pricing.

Commercial Times

item.title: China's market regulator ordered a record recall of about 4.3m vehicles from Tesla and up to ten other automakers, including Xiaomi and Xpeng, because flush electronic door handles may be hard to open and trap occupants in a crash and power loss.
item.description:
The State Administration for Market Regulation issued the recall on 21 August covering roughly 4.3 million cars, with Tesla alone accounting for about 2.98 million (Models 3, Y, X and S) to be fixed via software update. Regulators flagged that the fashionable flush handles — popularised by Tesla for a minimalist look and lower drag — can be difficult to operate in an emergency, and that interior mechanical release handles are often poorly marked and close in colour to the trim, hampering escape or rescue if power is lost after a collision. Nine to eleven brands are covered depending on the count. The action is China's largest coordinated auto recall and signals tighter regulatory scrutiny of a design feature that has spread across electric vehicles worldwide.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) and wider chemicals industry the exposure is indirect but real: the automotive sector is one of the largest markets for industrial adhesives, sealants, coatings and specialty polymers, and a regulator-driven rethink of door-handle design touches the assemblies, bonding and surface finishes those systems use. A record recall also adds cost and reputational pressure on carmakers already squeezed on margins, which tends to intensify supplier price negotiations. More broadly it shows China's market regulator willing to act at scale on product safety — a reminder for any supplier of automotive-grade materials to track evolving Chinese design and safety requirements.

MarketScreener | The New Indian Express | Xhby.net

item.title: The US ambassador to India says almost everything in the bilateral trade deal is agreed in principle and only legal text remains, with Secretary of State Rubio expected to visit in October; two-way trade is USD 240bn against a USD 500bn target.
item.description:
Washington signalled the pact is close. US ambassador Sergio Gor said "almost everything" about the US–India trade deal is done in principle and the remaining delay is legal and technical language, with the US "reconfiguring" some of the text. He tied the momentum to the personal rapport between Trump and Prime Minister Modi and said Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected in October. Bilateral goods-and-services trade has reached about USD 240bn — up from USD 20bn fifteen years ago — and the two governments have set a USD 500bn target for the coming years. A deal would ease the tariff uncertainty that has clouded Indian exporters and mark a contrast with the collapse of the US–Canada talks.

Industry Impact

India is a fast-growing market for construction, automotive and consumer-manufacturing demand that pulls through adhesives, coatings and sealants, so a US–India deal that lowers tariff risk supports the investment case there and could shift where global chemical majors source and expand. For ACS producers it points to firmer, more predictable trade lanes into a large emerging market at a time when North American and China-facing routes are getting harder. The practical watch-item is the final text — which sectors and tariff lines are covered — since that determines the real effect on chemical and industrial goods flows.

The Economic Times | The Times of India

item.title: With the EU's goods deficit with China topping EUR 1bn a day, German politicians are urging fast EU tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars, citing OECD findings that subsidies drive about 60% of China's export-share gains, as Europe weighs a wider response.
item.description:
Pressure for trade defence is building. Sebastian Lechner, CDU leader in Lower Saxony, called on the European Commission to impose import tariffs on Chinese hybrid cars "as soon as possible," pointing to OECD analysis that state subsidies underpin roughly 60% of the market share Chinese goods gain abroad — which he framed as a competitive distortion. European media report the Commission is already weighing countervailing duties on such vehicles. The debate is wider than autos: former EU trade chief Cecilia Malmström says the "China shock" concept is going global as Chinese factories out-produce sluggish domestic demand and flood export markets, and EU leaders have tasked the Commission with new trade-defence measures against a deficit that tops EUR 1bn a day. Beijing's Global Times warned that "protectionism is the last thing European automakers need," underscoring how contentious the step would be.

Industry Impact

Trade-defence action reshapes the competitive map for chemical and Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) producers on two fronts. New EU duties on Chinese vehicles would alter volumes and sourcing across the automotive supply chain — a core ACS end-market — and could invite Chinese retaliation that catches European exporters. More broadly, a structural EU turn toward barriers against Chinese goods signals rising input-cost volatility and shifting customer footprints, and follows the trade-defence duties China itself has been applying. ACS suppliers should track which product categories the Commission targets and prepare for a more fragmented, tariff-shaped Europe–China trade relationship.

Axios | Lianhe Zaobao | Bloomberg | Global Times

item.title: Germany's August manufacturing PMI jumped to 54.1, the strongest since early 2022, on rising output, orders and exports despite the low Rhine — but leading firms are pressing Chancellor Merz to speed up tax, pension, energy and deregulation reforms.
item.description:
The upside surprise was broad. S&P Global's flash manufacturing PMI — where readings above 50 signal expansion — rose to 54.1 from 52.2, well above the slight fall economists had expected, with production, new orders and exports all growing at their fastest since early 2022 even as low water on the Rhine constrained logistics. The recovery is now in its third consecutive quarter, and the cooperative-banking association BVR doubled its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1%. Yet the mood among industrialists remains impatient: seventeen signatories including Siemens, Audi, BMW, Porsche and supplier ZF wrote to Chancellor Friedrich Merz demanding faster action on high energy costs, taxes, pensions and red tape, and Merz plans to push his cabinet to implement pre-summer reform pledges quickly. Skilled-labour shortages are creeping back, with 23.2% of firms reporting a lack of qualified workers in July, up from 21.1% in April.

Industry Impact

Germany is the core European market for industrial adhesives, coatings and sealants, so a genuine manufacturing rebound supports demand across autos, machinery, electronics and construction after a long slump. The catch is that the recovery is fragile and cost-driven complaints persist — high energy prices and labour shortages squeeze the same industrial customers ACS suppliers serve and pressure their input budgets. The reform agenda (energy, deregulation, taxes) will shape how durable this upturn proves, so suppliers should treat the PMI bounce as an encouraging but not-yet-secured signal when planning German capacity and pricing.

Handelsblatt | WirtschaftsWoche | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | Handelsblatt

item.title: Treasury Secretary Bessent will announce the US plan to economically isolate Iran and its trading partners on 24 August; Tehran says it will halt all Gulf oil exports if the "economic war" proceeds, and China — the top buyer — is the key pressure point.
item.description:
The campaign moves from threat to detail today. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has scheduled a press conference for 24 August to set out secondary sanctions on any country that buys Iranian oil or handles its money, after President Trump billed the move an "economic D-Day" and the "most crushing" financial operation ever against Tehran. Iran's Supreme National Security Council warned that no oil will leave the Strait of Hormuz or the wider Gulf if the economic war goes ahead, and said any state assisting Washington would be treated as committing an act of war; Iranian officials also dismissed the sanctions as a sign of US "desperation." Beijing, which buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, has said sanctions will not solve anything and declined to help, raising the risk of US–China blowback. Oil prices eased on 24 August as traders awaited the specifics.

Industry Impact

The direct channel for the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry is energy and petrochemical feedstock costs: any credible threat to Hormuz flows or a real supply squeeze would lift the oil-linked inputs beneath most adhesives, coatings and sealants. The larger operational risk is the secondary-sanctions net — customers, suppliers or logistics partners with Iran links, especially in Asia, can be placed off-limits at short notice, so compliance screening and contract clauses need tightening now. A hardening US–China standoff over enforcement would also add uncertainty for firms with exposure to both markets.

LiveMint | The Economic Times | Commercial Times | Bjd.com.cn | Bloomberg | The New Indian Express

item.title: A near-final US–Canada deal collapsed before Friday's deadline after late US demands, triggering 50% US tariffs on about USD 20bn of Canadian goods on 22 August; Canada will retaliate dollar-for-dollar from 8 September.
item.description:
The tentative agreement fell apart less than an hour before the deadline. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Washington tried to rewrite terms at the last minute, so he recalled Canada's negotiators and rejected a deal that would have baked in permanent tariffs. According to reporting, the US sought a 4-million-tonne cap on Canadian steel with a 25% duty that doubled above it, wanted only US-made auto content exempted, and refused to cover forestry; Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had resisted cutting the car tariff to 15% for fear of undercutting US production. Washington then imposed 50% tariffs on roughly USD 20bn of Canadian exports — alcohol, electrical equipment, plywood, cement and more — on 22 August. Carney will match them "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, targeting US steel, dairy, paper, agricultural machinery, appliances and electronics. The US takes about 70% of Canada's exports, and officials warn more than USD 1tn of North American trade is now exposed.

Industry Impact

This removes the planning certainty a settled North American tariff line would have given chemical and Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) producers with cross-border plants and automotive, construction and packaging customers. Fifty-percent duties on inputs such as electrical equipment, plywood and cement raise costs across construction and manufacturing value chains, and Canada's retaliation on steel and machinery from September will feed through to equipment and building-materials prices on both sides of the border. Firms should map exposure on both tariff lists, stress-test contracts and pricing for a prolonged dispute, and watch for demand softening among automotive and construction customers if the trade war persists.

The Globe and Mail | The New York Times | POLITICO | Anadolu Agency | Anadolu Agency | CBC
